rules.statement: In production code, give every new or changed API an XML doc comment with a substantive `<summary>`.
rules.why: Documented API is part of the definition of done for production code.
rules.check: Look for new or changed public/protected members without `///` or with an empty or name-restating `<summary>`.

rules.statement: In production code, write documentation in the timeless present, describing what the code does, never what the change did.
rules.why: Docs outlive the change; history belongs in commits, not comments.
rules.check: Flag doc text like 'now', 'no longer', 'changed to', 'previously', 'new' that narrates the change.

rules.statement: In production code, write a `<summary>` across multiple lines, and open a property summary with "Gets or sets", "Gets" or "Sets" according to its accessors.
rules.why: Keeps doc comments uniform and accurate about accessor shape.
rules.check: Find single-line `<summary>...</summary>` tags and property summaries whose opening verb doesn't match the get/set accessors.

rules.statement: In production code comments, spell protocol terms in their specification casing ("JSON Web Token (JWT)", JSON, JOSE, OAuth, OpenID), not a .NET type's Pascal casing, while `cref`s and identifiers keep their real casing.
rules.why: Prose should match the specs readers know; type names belong only in code references.
rules.check: Search `///` and `//` prose for 'JsonWebToken', 'Jwt token', 'Oauth', 'OpenId' etc. used as prose rather than inside `<see cref>` or code.

rules.statement: In production code, never put internal citations (ADR numbers, decision-doc paths) in `///` doc comments; put them in a `//` line directly after the doc comment, above the declaration's attributes.
rules.why: Doc comments ship to consumers who can't follow internal references.
rules.check: Look for `ADR-\d{4}` or `docs/decisions/` inside `///` lines.

rules.statement: In production code, don't name internal implementation types or members in `///` doc comments of public API.
rules.why: Public docs should describe the contract, not internals consumers can't see or rely on.
rules.check: Check `///` text and `cref`s on public members for references to internal/private types or implementation details.

rules.statement: In production code, register OpenAPI document transformers (security schemes, tags, examples) in the composition layer's `AddOpenApi(...)` and expose the document and API-reference UI through the server's map extension, never re-declaring them in a host.
rules.why: The document describes the server's own endpoints, so its owner contributes to it once.
rules.check: Flag `AddOpenApi`, document transformers, `MapOpenApi` or API-reference UI mapping added in a host project.

rules.statement: In production code, never embed secret material in a served OpenAPI document or API-reference renderer configuration; pre-fill a secret only in Development, while wiring the login flow itself in every environment.
rules.why: Anyone who can load the reference page can read the served config; the bootstrap login flow must still work in production.
rules.check: Look for client secrets or passwords set in OpenAPI/renderer config without a Development-environment guard, or login flow configuration gated by environment.

rules.statement: In production code, to pre-fill an `x-www-form-urlencoded` field in an API-reference renderer, mark it `required` and set its schema `Default` in a document transformer rather than relying on a named example, and place credentials where the client's registered authentication method expects them.
rules.why: Renderers build form bodies from the schema; optional properties are omitted and examples aren't applied, and credentials in the wrong location fail authentication.
rules.check: Check OpenAPI transformers that try to pre-fill form fields via `example`, or renderer credential locations that don't match the client's registered auth method (e.g. `client_secret_basic` needs the Authorization header).

rules.statement: In production code, encode a password or secret into a sensitive `BufferFactory.Rent(…, isSensitive: true, out …)` rental via `SecureEncoding.UTF8` (`NCode.Buffers`), never `ArrayPool<byte>` plus manual zeroing, a bare `SecureMemoryPool<byte>.Shared` rental, or `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes`.
rules.why: Secret bytes must be pinned and zeroed on return so plaintext doesn't linger on the GC heap.
rules.check: Look for secret/password bytes produced by `Encoding.*.GetBytes`, `ArrayPool` with `CryptographicOperations.ZeroMemory`, or direct `SecureMemoryPool` use.

rules.statement: In production code, encode or decode a sensitive payload once at the earliest boundary and pass it down the call chain as `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, rather than re-encoding a `string` in a leaf method.
rules.why: Every extra encoding creates another copy of the secret.
rules.check: Find secret `string` parameters threaded through layers and encoded deep in a helper.

rules.statement: In production code, supply a secret that comes from configuration pre-encoded (Base64Url) and decode it straight into a secure buffer.
rules.why: A process-memory snapshot then doesn't expose the plaintext directly from the managed configuration string.
rules.check: Look for secrets read from configuration as plaintext strings and converted with a text encoding.

rules.statement: In production code, encode and decode text only through `SecureEncoding.UTF8`/`SecureEncoding.ASCII` (`NCode.Buffers`), never `Encoding.UTF8`, `Encoding.ASCII`, `Encoding.Default` or an overload that takes no encoding, and pass `contentEncoding: SecureEncoding.UTF8` to `TypedResults.Text`/`Content`.
rules.why: Strict encodings throw on invalid input, while the defaults silently substitute `?` or U+FFFD.
rules.check: Look for `Encoding.UTF8/ASCII/Default`, `File.ReadAllText(path)`, `new StreamReader(stream)`, `new StringContent(text)` without an encoding, or `TypedResults.Text` without `contentEncoding`.

rules.statement: In production code, have a producer of binary or key material write into a caller-supplied `ref TWriter` (`where TWriter : IBufferWriter<byte>, allows ref struct`) and accept `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`/`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` inputs instead of returning or taking `byte[]`.
rules.why: Avoids fresh array allocations and lets the caller control buffer lifetime and sensitivity.
rules.check: Flag new methods returning `byte[]` or taking `byte[]` parameters for binary data.

rules.statement: In production code, get a pooled writer from `BufferFactory.CreatePooledBufferWriter(isSensitive:)` (true for secrets) or `BufferFactory.CreateArrayBufferWriter()` for never-secret output, not a bare `ArrayBufferWriter<byte>`, `ArrayPool<T>.Shared`, `MemoryPool<T>.Shared` or `Sequence<T>`.
rules.why: `BufferFactory` makes sensitivity explicit and pins and zeroes secret buffers.
rules.check: Look for direct construction of `ArrayBufferWriter<T>`, `Sequence<T>` or use of shared pools.

rules.statement: In production code, read a multi-segment sequence segment by segment or with `SequenceReader<byte>`, taking one contiguous span with `GetSpanLease(isSensitive:)` only when a consumer needs it, and never by manual concatenation or `.ToArray()`.
rules.why: Concatenation and `.ToArray()` allocate and copy, and may leave secret copies behind.
rules.check: Look for `ReadOnlySequence<byte>.ToArray()` or loops that copy segments into a new array.

rules.statement: In production code, use a `BufferFactory` rental or a small fixed `stackalloc` for transient buffers, and use `new byte[]`, `.ToArray()`, `ArrayBufferWriter<T>` or `MemoryStream` only where an external API requires them, over a rented or pinned array obtained with `MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray`.
rules.why: Bare arrays allocate on the GC heap and can't be pinned or reliably zeroed.
rules.check: Flag `new byte[]`, `GC.AllocateArray`, `.ToArray()` or `MemoryStream` that no external API requires.

rules.statement: In production code, hold a secret kept in an object or across an `await` as a sensitive `BufferFactory.Rent(…, isSensitive: true, out Memory<byte>)` lease kept beside its memory, not as a `CreatePinnedArray` ref struct or a bare array.
rules.why: `CreatePinnedArray` returns a ref struct that works only synchronously within one method; the lease keeps the secure-pool array pinned and zeroes it on return.
rules.check: Look for secrets stored in fields or used across awaits as `byte[]`, or attempts to keep a pinned-array result beyond one synchronous method.

rules.statement: In production code, use the `BufferFactory.Rent` out-buffer at its returned length without slicing it back to the requested length, and prefer the `out Span<T>` overload, taking `out Memory<T>` only for a buffer stored in a field or used across an `await`.
rules.why: The out buffer is already exactly the requested length, and span is cheaper when memory isn't needed.
rules.check: Look for `.Slice(0, length)` or `[..length]` on a `Rent` result, or `out Memory<T>` used only synchronously within one method.

rules.statement: In production code, use a writable `Span<T>`/`Memory<T>` parameter only as a destination whose size the caller knows before the call (a fixed size, a sizing member beside it, or a length the caller chooses), return the count written when output can be shorter, and send output of unknown size to a `ref TWriter` writer.
rules.why: Callers must be able to size destinations correctly and know how much was written.
rules.check: Check new methods with writable span outputs for a sizing method or fixed size and a returned count.

rules.statement: In production code, a helper that rents and fills a buffer for its caller returns the lease plus a read-only view (`out ReadOnlySpan<T>`, or `out ReadOnlyMemory<T>` across an `await`), not a writable one.
rules.why: Only `BufferFactory.Rent` itself hands back writable memory; consumers shouldn't mutate filled output.
rules.check: Look for helpers returning a lease with `out Span<T>`/`out Memory<T>` of already-filled data.

rules.statement: In production code, split a compact JWS or JWE with `MemoryExtensions.Split` into a `stackalloc Range[segmentCount + 1]` and reject any count except `segmentCount`, never using `string.Split`.
rules.why: The spare slot makes extra segments push the count past the limit instead of folding into the last range, and nothing is allocated.
rules.check: Look for `string.Split('.')` on tokens, or a Range buffer sized exactly to the segment count.

rules.statement: In production code, take the JWS signing input as a slice of the original token text up to the end of the payload, never a re-concatenated string.
rules.why: Re-concatenation allocates and risks differing from the signed bytes.
rules.check: Look for `header + "." + payload` or similar string building for signature verification.

rules.statement: In production code, decode a base64url segment into a `BufferFactory.Rent` buffer sized by `Base64Url.GetByteCountForDecode`, and don't slice the result by `bytesWritten`, because `NCode.Base64Url` throws `FormatException` on invalid input.
rules.why: A strict decode that succeeds fills the buffer exactly.
rules.check: Look for decode buffers that are over-allocated and then sliced by bytesWritten, or base64url decoding that uses `Convert.FromBase64String`.

rules.statement: In production code, when an async method needs span work, do it in a synchronous helper.
rules.why: Spans and ref structs can't live across awaits.
rules.check: Look for async methods that convert to arrays or strings just to avoid span restrictions.

rules.statement: In production code, never hold sensitive text as a `string`: read key or secret files as bytes into a secure buffer (`File.OpenHandle` + `RandomAccess.Read`), and read or write sensitive XML with `XmlReader`/`XmlWriter` over a sensitive pooled buffer.
rules.why: Strings are immutable and can't be zeroed, so secrets linger in memory.
rules.check: Look for `File.ReadAllText`, `XDocument`/`ToString()` or other string APIs on key or secret material.

rules.statement: In production code, produce a `string` only for a non-secret value at a storage or wire boundary, exactly once, written in place with `string.Create`, never by renting a `char` buffer and copying it out with `new string(span)`.
rules.why: Avoids an extra allocation and copy.
rules.check: Look for `new string(span)` after filling a rented char buffer, or repeated intermediate strings on hot paths.

rules.statement: In production code, transform identifiers on hot paths into rented `char` spans (for example `MemoryExtensions.ToLowerInvariant(source, destination)`) instead of allocating new strings.
rules.why: Keeps hot paths free of avoidable allocations.
rules.check: Look for `string.ToLowerInvariant()`/`ToUpperInvariant()` on per-request paths.

rules.statement: In production code, when an interface implementation writes characters inside `string.Create`, check that `writer.WrittenCount == chars.Length`, and pass span inputs through an `internal readonly ref struct` state.
rules.why: This keeps a `'\0'` remainder from ever being persisted, and ref-struct state avoids copying.
rules.check: Check `string.Create` callbacks that delegate writing but don't verify the written count.

rules.statement: In production code, size a collection from a count you already know, and test `Count == 0` before a `foreach` over an interface-typed collection.
rules.why: This avoids regrowth and the allocation of a boxed enumerator for nothing on per-call paths.
rules.check: Look for `new List<T>()` or `new Dictionary<,>()` without a capacity when the count is known, and `foreach` over `IReadOnlyList`/`ICollection` on hot paths without an empty check.

rules.statement: Don't report readability problems in the inner loops of cryptographic or numeric primitives that use aggressive optimization (AggressiveInlining/Optimization, manual unrolling, `stackalloc`, `MemoryMarshal`/`Unsafe` reinterpretation); do report any optimization that adds a data-dependent branch or memory access to constant-time code, or that lacks passing test vectors.
rules.why: Speed takes priority over readability in these primitives, but constant-time behaviour and test-pinned correctness are never traded away.
rules.check: In math or crypto primitive changes, look for secret-dependent branches or indexing, missing test vectors, and a missing benchmark before/after in the PR.

rules.statement: In production code, a library never registers or removes a logging provider; only a host configures providers.
rules.why: Logging providers are the host's choice.
rules.check: Look for `ClearProviders`, `AddConsole` or other provider registration in library code.

rules.statement: In production code, log through source-generated `[LoggerMessage]` methods collected in a `Log` class marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, with constant message templates that use named placeholders.
rules.why: Source-generated logging is allocation-free, and the generated plumbing shouldn't count toward coverage.
rules.check: Look for `logger.LogInformation(...)`-style calls, interpolated templates, or a `Log` class without `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`.

rules.statement: In production code, a shipping package never depends on `Microsoft.Extensions.Telemetry.Abstractions` (including through `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`) or sets `DisableMicrosoftExtensionsLoggingSourceGenerator`; bound outbound calls with `Polly.Core` instead.
rules.why: Those dependencies replace the consumers' `[LoggerMessage]` generator.
rules.check: Check package references and MSBuild properties in packable projects.

rules.statement: In production code, define event IDs as named constants in a per-package `internal static class EventIds`, as `Base + n` from a `private const int Base`, each named exactly like its `[LoggerMessage]` method.
rules.why: Gives every event a stable, discoverable ID.
rules.check: Look for literal EventId numbers in `[LoggerMessage]`, or constants whose names don't match their method.

rules.statement: In production code, give each runtime package a disjoint family-wide event-ID band, never renumber or reuse a shipped event ID, and don't log from `*.Abstractions` packages.
rules.why: Globally unique, stable IDs let operators key filters and alerts on a number regardless of the emitting assembly; abstractions have no behavior to log.
rules.check: Look for changed values of existing event IDs, IDs outside the package's band, or logging in an abstractions package.

rules.statement: In production code, measure each signal once through its owner: enrich `http.server.request.duration` through `IHttpMetricsTagsFeature` rather than adding a duplicate request instrument, and add a new instrument only for a mechanism of your own.
rules.why: Telemetry has one owner per signal, so nothing is double counted.
rules.check: Look for new counters or histograms that duplicate ASP.NET Core request metrics or existing event counters.

rules.statement: In production code, create meters through `IMeterFactory` and keep a package's instruments in one internal metrics singleton.
rules.why: DI-created meters are testable and are disposed with their scope.
rules.check: Look for `new Meter(...)` or instruments scattered across classes.

rules.statement: In production code, never use an unbounded or identifying value (tenant, client, subject, address, handle) as a metric attribute or span attribute; take attribute values from a vocabulary the server controls.
rules.why: This keeps cardinality bounded and keeps identifiers out of telemetry.
rules.check: Inspect tags added to instruments and activities for IDs, addresses or user-supplied strings.

rules.statement: In production code, give count instruments a `{noun}` unit.
rules.why: Follows OpenTelemetry unit conventions.
rules.check: Check the unit argument of new counters.

rules.statement: In production code, cover every metric instrument with a test that uses `MetricCollector<T>`.
rules.why: Instruments are part of the observable contract.
rules.check: For each new instrument, look for a matching `MetricCollector<T>` test.

rules.statement: In production code, trace only your own mechanisms, through one `ActivitySource` per package named like its meter.
rules.why: Spans mirror their owner's instruments and don't duplicate framework spans.
rules.check: Look for multiple ActivitySources per package, names that differ from the meter, or spans wrapping framework operations already traced.

rules.statement: In production code, model configuration as a strongly-typed options class in an `Options/` folder; use `IOptions<T>` for values fixed at startup and `IOptionsMonitor<T>` for values that change at runtime.
rules.why: Typed options give one validated shape for configuration and the right change semantics.
rules.check: Look for raw `IConfiguration` reads, options outside `Options/`, or a mismatched options interface.

rules.statement: In production code, apply the same validation rule to configured data and to the same data written at runtime (for example through a management API).
rules.why: Otherwise runtime writes could store values configuration would reject.
rules.check: Check that a new validation for configured data is also called on runtime write paths, and the reverse.

rules.statement: In production code, have each strategy validate its own options.
rules.why: The strategy owns the meaning of its options.
rules.check: Look for central validators checking options that belong to a specific strategy.

rules.statement: In production code, derive a default for runtime-written data through the seam that judges it, then validate and store it like an explicit value.
rules.why: Defaults must pass the same rules as explicit values.
rules.check: Look for write paths that fill defaults inline or skip validation for defaulted values.

rules.statement: In production code, make a configuration seeder require an explicit identifier for the target it seeds rather than assuming one.
rules.why: A seeder names exactly the target it seeds.
rules.check: Look for seeder options with an optional or implicit target ID.

rules.statement: In production code, validate an options period that is handed to a timer when the host starts, with `TimerPeriod.IsValid`.
rules.why: An invalid timer period should fail at startup, not at runtime.
rules.check: Look for timer-period options without startup validation.
